clue.text: Backed up very loudly, creating smoke

indicators.note: something backed is moved backwards, so the word 'up' is read from its end

parts.note: the word taken as it stands, ready to be turned round
ff, fortissimo, is the musical marking for very loud

explanation.surface: A car or a drain backs up with a loud bang and belches out smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed up' reads as one phrase, like a blocked pipe; split it and 'Backed' is the instruction applied to 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: To puff on a pipe or cigarette is to draw on it, a plain verb synonym for smoking.

clue.text: Information for delivery company engaged in job from Parisian

indicators.note: someone engaged in work is inside it, so the company sits within the job

parts.note: a post is a job or position
the standard abbreviation for company
de is French for 'from'

explanation.surface: A courier firm hires a Frenchman and wants details for its deliveries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Delivery company' looks like one unit, a courier; the definition actually ends at 'delivery' and 'company' belongs to the wordplay. A POSTCODE is the British equivalent of a ZIP code.
explanation.definitionFit: The postcode on an envelope is the address detail that sorting offices use to route letters and parcels.

clue.text: Tear sock, worn at the bottom and shabby

parts.note: to tear is to rush along, to fly
a sock is a punch, a blow

indicators.note: in a down entry the bottom of a word is its final letter, so only the end of 'worn' is kept

parts.note: the last letter of 'worn'

explanation.surface: A sock with a hole worn through its sole looks tatty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tear' and 'sock' both read as a ripped piece of hosiery; each is really a verb or noun of violence and speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Flyblown literally means tainted by flies' eggs, and is extended to anything dingy, squalid or run-down.

clue.text: Without right, William I's lot obtain neutral territory

indicators.note: 'without' asks for the group named next to lose the letter standing for 'right'

parts.note: R is the usual abbreviation for right; it is the letter removed
William the Conqueror's people were the Normans, here minus one letter
to land a job is to obtain it

explanation.surface: A history-book line about the Norman conquest grabbing land without any legal right.
explanation.walkthrough: William I is William the Conqueror, whose Normans invaded England in 1066; take R out of NORMANS.
explanation.definitionFit: No man's land is the strip between opposing front lines that neither army holds, hence ground belonging to nobody.

clue.text: Variant bug originally deleted

indicators.note: the original, first letter of the word for 'bug' is the one struck out

parts.note: to bug someone is to annoy or bother them

explanation.surface: A software note: the variant of the code with the bug was removed at source.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests computing or virus variants; 'bug' is simply the verb 'annoy'.
explanation.definitionFit: A variant is a different or alternative version, so 'other' serves as its adjective synonym.

clue.text: Tech giant triumvirate in need of hot growth

parts.note: Apple, the computer and phone company

indicators.note: to be in need of something is to lack it, so the letter for 'hot' is missing from the group of three

parts.note: a triumvirate is a ruling group of three
H for hot, as on a tap; this letter goes

explanation.surface: A big tech company's leadership trio needs a hot spell of growth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Growth' looks like business jargon for the tech giant; it is the definition, meaning something that grows.
explanation.definitionFit: A tree is a plant, and plants are often called growths in crossword usage, here one that bears fruit.

clue.text: Dairy food that's highly processed?

parts.note: surface reading: a dairy product full of additives and industrial treatment
setter's reading: made high up, in Alpine dairies among the mountains

explanation.walkthrough: 'Highly processed' is the health-food warning on junk food; read 'highly' as 'at altitude' and it points to a cheese made in the Alps.
explanation.definitionFit: Emmental and Gruyère come from mountain pastures in Switzerland, so this cheese is literally produced at great height.

clue.text: Portion of contemporary art sale's returns missing

indicators.note: something that returns goes back, so the concealed run is read right to left
a portion is a part, so the letters sit inside the words that follow

parts.note: the run straddling the end of 'contemporary', all of 'art' and the start of 'sale's'

explanation.surface: Some of the takings from a modern-art auction have gone unaccounted for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Returns' reads as financial returns from the sale; here it is the instruction to read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gone astray has wandered off or been lost, the same as being absent or unaccounted for.

clue.text: Stewart, say, making a comeback with group somewhere in England

indicators.note: a comeback is a return, so Stewart's first name runs backwards

parts.note: Rod Stewart, the rock singer, is an example of a Rod
a set is a group

explanation.surface: Rod Stewart plans a comeback tour with a band somewhere in England.
explanation.walkthrough: A singer 'making a comeback with group' is a natural showbiz story. Dorset is a county on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorset is a county of southern England, so it is one example of a place located in that country.

clue.text: Course in mythology gets bogged down during lecture

indicators.note: a lecture is spoken out loud, so we want a word that is heard rather than seen

parts.note: something bogged down sticks fast

explanation.surface: A mythology course gets stuck in the mud halfway through a lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Course' looks academic, like the lecture; it is a watercourse, a river.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the Styx is the river the dead cross into the underworld, so a waterway from legend.

clue.text: Thief, grass and long-term felon receiving time

parts.note: to grass or shop someone is to inform on them to the police

indicators.note: the lifelong prisoner takes in, or receives, the letter for 'time'

parts.note: a prisoner serving a life sentence
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A roll call of the criminal underworld: a thief, an informer and a lifer doing time.
explanation.walkthrough: Grass and shop are British slang for informing on someone; LIFER wraps round T.
explanation.definitionFit: A shoplifter steals goods from shops, a particular kind of thief.

clue.text: Common complaint, flipping crude relations being super-cool

parts.note: the common cold, an everyday ailment

indicators.note: flipping something over turns it round, so the word for 'crude' goes backwards

parts.note: raw means crude or unrefined

explanation.surface: A grumble about crude relatives who act as though they are too cool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive attached to 'crude relations'; it reverses 'crude' alone, and 'relations' starts the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cold War was the long period of frosty hostility between the Soviet bloc and the West without open fighting.

clue.text: Pay-outs accompanied by article going into slurs

parts.note: 'with' means accompanied by

indicators.note: the article goes into the slurs, so it ends up placed inside that word

parts.note: a drawl is a slow, slurred way of speaking
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Compensation payments made after a newspaper article carried slurs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slurs' looks like libel from the article, which makes the pay-outs damages; it is slurred speech.
explanation.definitionFit: Withdrawals are sums of money taken out of a bank account, and so paid out to the holder.

clue.text: Subject in jeans sold a TV set, nothing odd about that

indicators.note: none of the odd-placed characters are wanted, leaving only the even ones

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on of that phrase

explanation.surface: Someone sold a television while dressed in jeans, and there is nothing strange about that.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Subject' is a verb here, as in to subject a nation, not a topic.
explanation.definitionFit: To subject a people is to bring them under control and rule, which in its extreme form means making them slaves.

clue.text: Hard-headed fuzz stop overlooking outsiders by den

parts.note: fuzz is soft fine hair or fluff, down

indicators.note: to overlook is to ignore, so the outside letters of 'stop' are left out

parts.note: the two middle letters of 'stop'
an earth is a fox's den

explanation.surface: Tough police stop and ignore the people hanging around outside a drug den.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fuzz' is slang for police and the surface leans on it; here it is fluffy down.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hard-headed is practical and unsentimental, which is what calling a person realistic and grounded means.

clue.text: One comes bearing chocolates for a special date

definitions.text: One comes bearing chocolates for a special date

parts.words: One comes bearing chocolates for a special date
parts.note: surface reading: a suitor arrives with a box of chocolates for a romantic evening out

parts.words: One comes bearing chocolates for a special date
parts.note: setter's reading: a hollow confection, often packed with small sweets inside, given on a spring festival day

explanation.walkthrough: 'Date' pulls towards romance, with the one bearing chocolates a person; the special date is a day in the church calendar, and the thing carrying chocolates is itself chocolate.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocolate eggs given at the Christian spring festival often contain further sweets inside the shell.

clue.text: Most cracked up as fleapit's opening with funny talkies

indicators.note: the opening of a word is its first character, so only the start of 'fleapit' counts

parts.note: first letter of 'fleapit'

indicators.note: funny means peculiar here, so the letters of 'talkies' are rearranged

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: An audience in a shabby cinema laughs hardest when it shows comic films.
explanation.walkthrough: A fleapit is British slang for a run-down cinema, and talkies are early sound films; 'cracked up' suggests laughing, but means crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaky is slang for eccentric or unreliable, close to crackers, and the superlative matches 'most'.

clue.text: One with depression — it is linked with variable sense of self

parts.note: Roman numeral for one
a dent is a small depression in a surface
the word itself
y is a standard algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A psychology note: depression is linked with an unstable sense of self.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depression' and 'variable' sound clinical; one is a hollow in metal, the other a maths letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A person's identity is who they understand themselves to be, their individual character and selfhood.

clue.text: She-Devil broadcast directed in a mess

indicators.note: to broadcast is to scatter widely, as seed is sown, so the letters are strewn about

parts.note: anagram fodder, eight letters
to direct is to lead

explanation.surface: A TV screening of the drama She-Devil, directed chaotically.
explanation.walkthrough: She-Devil was a 1980s BBC drama, later a film, so 'broadcast' and 'directed' feel like TV credits.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishevelled describes untidy hair or clothes, someone looking rumpled and messy.

clue.text: Shot on top of second drink causes gas

parts.note: a shot is an attempt, a go
s is the abbreviation for second
a sip is a small drink

explanation.surface: Downing a shot on top of another drink gives you wind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On top of' just places the first piece above the rest in a down entry. Gas is idle chatter.
explanation.definitionFit: To gas is to chat at length about trivia, and gossip is idle talk, so the two share an informal verb sense.

clue.text: Check for every benefit

parts.note: per means for each, as in ten pounds per head
use is benefit or advantage, as in 'what's the use?'

explanation.surface: An instruction to check eligibility for every welfare benefit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check for' looks like one verb phrase; 'for' belongs with 'every'.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse a document is to read or examine it carefully, looking through it to inspect its contents.

clue.text: Manage within budget — a repossession's coming around

indicators.note: coming around means turning about, so the concealed run is read backwards
the letters lie inside the words that follow

parts.note: the end of 'budget', the 'a', and the start of 'repossession's'

explanation.surface: Advice to live within your means because the bailiffs are on their way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Within budget' looks like a set phrase for spending sensibly; 'within' is the pointer to letters hiding inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To operate a business or machine is to run it or control it, a plain verb synonym.

clue.text: Little pickle beginning to grate with that woman's family

indicators.note: a beginning is a start, so only the first character of 'grate' is used

parts.note: the first letter of 'grate'
the possessive 'her'
kin are one's relatives

explanation.surface: A naughty child, a little pickle, starts to annoy a woman's relatives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little pickle' is an affectionate British term for a mischievous child, which is where the surface goes; the answer is a small pickled cucumber.
explanation.definitionFit: A gherkin is a small cucumber preserved in vinegar, a literal miniature pickle.

clue.text: Relative will eat nothing and grumble

indicators.note: to eat something is to take it inside, so the relative swallows the zero

parts.note: a gran is a grandmother
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A fussy relation refuses to eat anything and complains.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eat nothing' reads as refusing food; the relative literally eats the letter for nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: To groan is to complain or moan about something, the same informal verb sense as grumbling.

clue.text: Part of a kennel club, perhaps, that's short of members?

definitions.text: Part of a kennel club, perhaps, that's short of members?

parts.note: surface reading: a club struggling to recruit enough people to join
setter's reading: a breed whose limbs are stubby, a canine with very short legs

explanation.walkthrough: Members are limbs as well as club joiners. The Kennel Club is the body that registers British dog breeds; a sausage dog is a dachshund.
explanation.definitionFit: The dachshund is a long, low breed with famously stumpy legs, nicknamed for its elongated body shape.

clue.text: Idle frolics in store

indicators.note: to frolic is to romp about playfully, so the letters of 'idle' jump around

parts.note: anagram fodder, four letters

explanation.surface: A lazy worker messes about in the shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Idle' reads as the lazy shop worker, but it is only the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A deli, short for delicatessen, is a shop selling cooked meats, cheeses and prepared foods.

clue.text: Campaign with alpha male who has media contacts?

parts.note: to press for something is to campaign for it
alpha is A in the phonetic alphabet
a gent is a gentleman, a man

explanation.surface: An election campaign run by a macho type with friends in the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a descriptive phrase, 'one who has media contacts', with the question mark flagging the loose fit.
explanation.definitionFit: A press agent is employed to handle publicity, so their job depends on knowing journalists and editors.

clue.text: King and Queen got out of celebrity-style visit

indicators.note: the royal pair get out of the word, leaving it without their letters

parts.note: starry means like a star, glamorous
R for rex, Latin for king; removed
R for regina, Latin for queen; removed

explanation.surface: The King and Queen step out of the car for a glitzy state visit.
explanation.walkthrough: R stands for both rex and regina, so both Rs come out of STARRY.
explanation.definitionFit: A stay is a period spent as a guest somewhere, the same as a visit, both nouns.
